articles.title: The Beatles Belong to Us
articles.author: Alex Niven
articles.content_excerpt: As we enter the late 2020s, the legacy of the Beatles — history’s biggest band, by any measure — is facing a final reckoning. Paul McCartney and Ringo Starr, the group’s last surviving members, are now eighty-four and eighty-six, respectively. This should remind us that what might be called the “Beatles generation” is reaching the end of its natural lifespan, its icons departing the stage to become musty archival heritage. All things, as the late George Harrison once acknowledged, must pass.Partly as a result, the second half of the decade looks set to be a heyday of fabology (that is, critical appraisal of the Fab Four). articles.title: Corporation Pop
articles.content_excerpt: In 2012, South Korean rapper and singer-songwriter PSY released a K-pop track called “Gangnam Style.” A month after its release, the song was viral — it peaked at number two on the US’s Billboard Hot 100 and topped charts in 30 other countries around the world, while the accompanying music video snagged Best Video at the MTV Europe Music Awards and became the first YouTube video to clock one billion views, subsequently maintaining its record as the most viewed YouTube video for the next five years. articles.title: Trump’s World Cup
articles.author: Juliet Jacques
articles.content_excerpt: The 2026 World Cup was supposed to provide relief from the tournament’s bedevilment by autocratic regimes, following the outrage that greeted FIFA’s selection of Russia for 2018 host and Qatar for 2022. As it happened, hosting rights were awarded to the United States, Canada, and Mexico in 2018, during Donald Trump’s first term, in a process delayed by the scandal that forced FIFA president Sepp Blatter to resign and be replaced by Gianni Infantino. The tournament was intended to promote unity among the North American nations, even if most of it would happen in the United States. But hopes that it would prove less charged than recent World Cups were dashed when Trump returned to power in January 2025, threatening to attack Mexico and invade Canada. articles.title: In North Korea, the Spurs Would’ve Won the Finals
articles.content_excerpt: In October 1996, North Korean leader Kim Jong Il issued an order encouraging basketball in schools and government organs. The following January, he published a treatise called “We Must Put Efforts to Developing Basketball.” Over the next two years, he required every high school and military squad to field a team, and he ordered counties, cities, and provincial people’s committees to build basketball facilities, along with gymnasiums at military schools. Out of that campaign came an independent set of rules. The country’s basketball association said it was meant to promote the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea’s independence and the popularity of the game. articles.title: The Really, Really Short Twenty-First Century
articles.author: David Broder
articles.content_excerpt: A few months ago, my partner and I met a liberal, fortysomething history professor who told us that for his next book he’d been reading up on late-1990s alter-globalization movements. As the millennium neared, global capitalism seemingly stood unchallenged. Social democrats and ex-communists praised the free market, and groupings like the World Trade Organization (WTO) integrated Russian and Chinese leaders. Yet this, he had discovered, wasn’t the whole story. It turned out that each of these elite conferences had been confronted by mass protests calling for an alternative global community. This rainbow coalition hadn’t detailed exactly what it wanted. But it had, he said, a world-changing ambition hard to find on today’s Left. articles.content_excerpt: Finish the American Revolution Jacobin ’s latest print issue is a welcome addition to the growing conversation about the need for a new and democratic constitution. articles.title: Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan Now Have Their Own NATO
articles.author: Annelle Sheline
articles.content_excerpt: On August 7, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey announced a mutual defense pact called the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement. Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan compared the arrangement to NATO, specifically citing Article 5’s collective defense clause. President Donald Trump lauded the pact as a “BIG, BOLD, IMPORTANT FIRST STEP” toward ensuring countries in the Middle East “will finally be able to defend themselves.” On this point, he’s largely right. What he failed to mention is that this shift reflects the growing realization that the United States and Israel are the most significant drivers of instability in the Middle East. articles.title: West Indian Cricketers Refused to Grovel
articles.author: Meagan Day
articles.content_excerpt: The summer of 1976 was Britain’s hottest in 350 years. The West Indies cricket team was there all season long, playing England in city after city in the oppressive heat. There was a lot riding on its performance. To the cricketers and their fans back home in the Caribbean, the team’s mission went beyond athletics. Though the West Indies had produced some legendary international cricketers and won stirring victories, its players were often condescendingly referred to as “calypso cricketers,” meaning they were entertaining but not particularly serious. Now they intended to prove themselves a capable force in the sport. articles.title: US Empire Has Strangled Cuba
articles.content_excerpt: In 1950, as conservatives are keen to point out, Cuba was among the better-off societies in Latin America. Its income per person was ahead of the Dominican Republic’s. Today, by that same measure, the Dominican Republic is more than twice as rich as Cuba. However, something happened to Cuba that did not happen to its neighbors — not just a 1959 socialist revolution but a US blockade, in force since 1962.What makes Cuba’s trajectory remarkable is not simply the income gap with its peer nations but what the country achieved in spite of it. Cuban life expectancy, nine years behind that of the United States in 1950, drew level with it by the early 1980s. Infant mortality fell below the US rate around the turn of the century. articles.title: Europe’s Far Right Kisses the Ring
articles.author: Jacopo Custodi
articles.content_excerpt: For years, Europe’s rising far-right parties have wrapped themselves in the language of sovereignty. Draped in their respective national flags, each has promised to put national interests and national identity above all else. France’s Rassemblement National deploys the slogan “Les Français d’abord,” meaning “the French first,” while Germany’s Alternative für Deutschland follows suit with “Deutschland zuerst.” In her first postelection speech, Giorgia Meloni, leader of Italy’s governing party, Fratelli d’Italia, promised to “start from national interests,” asserting it as a bedrock principle from which all other considerations must flow. articles.title: David and Goliath
articles.content_excerpt: The motor of an Iranian Shahed-136 drone is little more powerful or complex than that of a motorcycle. But stopping one is no simple matter, as the United States and Israel found out after they launched a war on Iran in February. To protect Israel and the Gulf states from Iran’s cheap, mass-produced drones, the United States had to fire off thousands of sophisticated, scarce interceptors. Over the course of the conflict, some $26.1 billion worth of munitions disappeared into the sky, potentially leaving the United States with too few interceptors to sustain its security commitments around the world. articles.title: Ibrahim Traoré Would Like to Be Thomas Sankara’s Heir
articles.author: Bettina Engels
articles.content_excerpt: Ibrahim Traoré, president of Burkina Faso since October 2022, polarizes opinion, to say the least. Some hail him as the hope for a new Pan-Africanism, the long-overdue end of French imperialism in West Africa, and resource sovereignty. Others point to the authoritarian traits of the regime and the repression of trade unionists, civil society activists, and journalists. The scope of Traoré’s political projects, and the pace at which they are being implemented, is striking. This has generated enthusiasm, particularly among a younger generation that vehemently rejects French neocolonial dominance and is deeply frustrated by a gerontocratic political system unable or unwilling to deliver reform. articles.title: From Solar Panels to State Terrorism
articles.content_excerpt: In 2022 and 2023, the United Arab Emirates (UAE) promised African nations $97 billion worth of investment in ports, energy, mining, agriculture, communications, manufacturing, real estate, and more.
